## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure is one of the largest concentrated capital commitments of the 2020s. Combined capital expenditure by the leading AI laboratories and their compute partners is projected to reach \$660--690 billion in 2026.^[Sources: Amazon FY2026 capital-expenditure guidance (CNBC, February 5, 2026); Alphabet Q4 2025 earnings release (SEC EDGAR, exhibit 99.1); Microsoft FY2026 Q2 earnings release.] OpenAI's Stargate joint venture with SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX alone commits up to \$500 billion in U.S. AI infrastructure through 2029, with an initial deployment of \$100 billion.^[\url{https://openai.com/index/announcing-the-stargate-project/}.]^[The centrality of compute to AI capability has made it a focal point for governance: governments and firms increasingly use compute allocation, monitoring, and export controls as levers for AI safety and industrial policy; see @sastry2024computing on compute as an instrument of AI governance.] These investments are largely irreversible, yet the uncertainty driving them, whether and when AI capabilities will reach a transformative threshold, remains unresolved. This paper asks how a firm should time, size, and allocate an irreversible capacity investment when the return to that capacity depends on a regime change whose arrival is uncertain and whose competitive consequences hinge on how the capacity was used before it arrived.

A frontier AI laboratory produces intelligence by combining two forms of compute. *Training compute* is used to optimize a neural network's parameters on massive datasets, yielding a model whose quality scales as a power law of compute invested [@kaplan2020scaling; @altman2025observations]. *Inference compute* runs the trained model to serve predictions and generate revenue. Both activities consume the same scarce hardware: purpose-built GPU clusters housed in multi-billion-dollar data centers. This creates an allocation problem that standard capital budgeting does not address: the same asset can either produce revenue now or build the capability that determines the firm's position in a future that may not arrive.^[In practice, AI infrastructure investment also encompasses substantial expenditure on power generation and transmission (dedicated natural gas plants, long-term power purchase agreements, on-site substations) required to supply the hundreds of megawatts that a single training cluster demands. For tractability, I model all of these complementary investments as a single capital outlay in "compute capacity," with the cost function $I(K) = cK^\gamma$ absorbing the full cost of bringing a unit of capacity online, including its power supply.]

These facilities take years to build, and the capacity they add is costly to redirect once installed. Large-scale training clusters involve substantial configuration, networking, and software investments that create adjustment costs when reallocating compute between training and inference, even though the underlying GPU hardware is physically fungible.

Executives frame the resulting risk calculus in asymmetric terms. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai has argued that "the risk of underinvesting is dramatically greater than the risk of overinvesting,"^[Alphabet Q2 2024 earnings call, July 2024.] while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contends that agentic AI and reasoning require "easily 100x more" compute than anticipated just one year prior.^[Nvidia GTC 2025 keynote, March 2025.] The prize these investments target is Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): a step change in model capability sufficient to automate a broad range of cognitive tasks and generate sustained, qualitatively higher demand for compute [@amodei2024machines]. Executive forecasts of its arrival run from "superintelligence in a few thousand days" [@altman2024intelligence] and 2026--2027 [@amodei2024machines], through "AGI in 2026,"^[Elon Musk, post on X, 2025: \url{https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2025124840806514916}.] to "not with current architectures."^[PYMNTS, "Meta: Large Language Models Will Not Get to Human-Level Intelligence," 2025.] Firms must therefore commit irreversible capital under widely different priors about the same event.

Existing frameworks illuminate parts of this problem but not its core difficulty. Real-options models [@mcdonald1986value; @dixit1994investment] characterize irreversibility and timing but take the use of installed capacity as given; R&D race models [@loury1979market; @reinganum1982strategic] capture competitive intensity but treat pre-breakthrough expenditure as pure cost with no concurrent revenue; structural credit models [@leland1994corporate] handle leverage and default, and a branch of that literature already embeds regime switching, but they take the size of the growth option as exogenous rather than as a capacity-allocation choice. What is missing is the interaction among these forces. A firm's decision to bet on the future by allocating capacity to training simultaneously weakens its ability to survive to that future by diverting capacity from revenue-generating inference. This tension makes the investment problem different from standard capacity choice: the option to grow and the risk of failure are not merely coexistent but mechanically linked through the same allocation decision.

This paper develops a model that places this allocation problem at the center of the investment decision. A firm chooses when to invest, how much capacity to install, and what fraction to devote to training versus inference, facing regime-switching demand [@guo2005investment], duopoly preemption [@grenadier2002option; @huisman2015strategic], endogenous default [@leland1994corporate], and diminishing returns to capacity, with the curvature parameter calibrated to empirical scaling laws [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training]. The primary contribution is the identification and characterization of the training-survival channel: because the same capacity serves both current revenue and future capability, the allocation decision links a firm's growth option value to its default boundary, producing mechanisms (faith-based survival, asymmetric belief costs, and a training allocation pinned by beliefs rather than market position) that the component models do not generate individually. The results fall into three categories.

First, I characterize the optimal training fraction, investment trigger, and capacity analytically. The firm chooses not only when to invest and how much capacity to install, but how to split that capacity between model training, which builds capability for the future, and inference serving, which generates revenue today. In regime $L$, the current low-demand regime, revenue depends on inference capacity through a Tullock contest, in which a firm's revenue share equals its share of industry inference capacity; in regime $H$, the post-AGI regime, revenue depends on training quality. This regime-specific competition creates a strategic trade-off absent from standard capacity models: a firm that allocates too much to training sacrifices current revenue and risks default, while a firm that allocates too little sacrifices its competitive position once AGI arrives. Duopoly preemption operates on the timing margin: at baseline volatility, and conditional on the convention that the leader installs the monopoly-phase optimal scale, the leader invests at a trigger roughly 43\% below the monopoly benchmark. It does not operate on the allocation margin. Because the regime-specific contests depend on the same relative capacities when allocations are common, the contest shares cancel from the allocation first-order condition, and leader, follower, and monopolist all choose the same training fraction.

Second, the interaction of training allocation with leverage and default risk produces a *faith-based survival* mechanism: training investment raises the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}$ through the expected post-AGI continuation value, lowering the default boundary. The same allocation raises the loss given default, because a larger training fraction shrinks the inference business creditors can liquidate: the continuation value that keeps the firm alive is worthless to creditors in bankruptcy. The survival channel operates only in parameter regions where it dominates current cash-flow weakness, a condition I characterize in closed form for the symmetric duopoly.

Third, I quantify the cost of *Dario's dilemma*, the loss a firm incurs by investing on a belief about the AGI arrival intensity $\lambda$ that differs from its true value. If a firm invests as though AGI were less likely to arrive than it is, it invests too late and loses first-mover advantage; if it invests as though AGI were more likely, it overbuilds and risks default. The training allocation sharpens both sides: a pessimistic firm under-allocates to training and forgoes most of the post-AGI option value, while an optimistic firm over-allocates and sacrifices the inference revenue it needs to survive. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei describes the overbuilding side: "I could buy \$1 trillion of compute that starts at the end of 2027... there's no hedge on Earth that could stop me from going bankrupt" [@amodei2026dwarkesh]. In a stylized calibration to four AI lab archetypes, the asymmetry can be substantial (Numerical Finding 1): investing as though $\lambda = 0.02$ when the true intensity is $0.10$ costs roughly 26\% of firm value, against about 6\% for investing as though $\lambda = 0.20$. The dilemma is nonetheless two-sided, because overinvestment concentrates risk in the tail: at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.50$ and leverage $\ell = 0.40$, the five-year default probability is nearly eight times its value under correct beliefs.

The model focuses on duopoly as the core strategic setting. Frontier AI training competition appears highly concentrated: on public accounts, the largest training runs to date have been conducted by a handful of laboratories, often backed by or partnered with a single cloud provider (e.g., Anthropic--Amazon, OpenAI--Microsoft) or building proprietary clusters (e.g., xAI's Colossus). The dominant strategic margin is not atomistic competition but rivalry among a few labs, each making multi-billion-dollar capacity commitments. Duopoly is the minimal model that captures the key forces (strategic preemption, race-like training allocation incentives, and continuation-value effects under leverage) while maintaining analytical tractability.^[An $N>2$ extension along the lines of @bouis2009multistage may be feasible but would sacrifice the closed-form characterization that makes the duopoly results transparent.]

{{< include _literature.qmd >}}

The paper proceeds as follows. @sec-model presents the model environment with training-inference allocation, regime switching, the single-firm benchmark, and the duopoly equilibrium with default risk; the analytical and semi-analytical results are contained in this section. @sec-calibration describes the stylized calibration to frontier AI lab archetypes and presents baseline numerical results. @sec-valuation develops quantitative implications: credit risk and Dario's dilemma. @sec-discussion considers policy implications, testable predictions, and limitations. @sec-conclusion concludes. The Internet Appendix collects the proofs, the numerical verification methods, the calibration sources, and the robustness exercises, together with several supporting figures.
